result: The EMTA biosensor platform was developed using ebBRET to monitor G protein activation through effector translocation (Gi/o, Gq/11, G12/13), Gαs dissociation from the plasma membrane, and βarrestin recruitment. The platform does not require modification of receptors or G proteins except for Gs.
evaluation: Claims C7-C10 and C17-C19 describe the core design principles of the EMTA platform with supporting experimental data shown in Figures 1A-B. The mechanism is clearly illustrated and the requirement for Gαs tagging is explicitly acknowledged, providing a complete description of the platform architecture.

result: The selectivity and specificity of EMTA biosensors for different G protein families were validated using pharmacological inhibitors (UBO-QIC for Gq/11, PTX for Gi/o) and genetic knockout cell lines, demonstrating family-specific responses with known exceptions (Gαz insensitive to PTX, Gα15 insensitive to UBO-QIC).
evaluation: Claims C20-C32 present comprehensive validation data shown in Figure 2A-C and supplementary figures. The use of both pharmacological tools and genetic knockouts provides orthogonal validation. The known exceptions (C22, C26) are properly cited and the effector selectivity (C32) is demonstrated experimentally.

result: Overexpression of G proteins, GPCRs, or effector-RlucII components did not affect the potency (pEC50) of responses in the heterologous expression system, and competition with endogenous G proteins did not occur to a significant extent.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 and C110-C112 are supported by titration experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary files 1B-D. The data demonstrate that varying expression levels of system components affects amplitude but not potency, validating the robustness of the assay configuration.

result: EMTA enables real-time imaging of G protein effector recruitment to the plasma membrane, providing spatiotemporal resolution for detecting Gαi/o, Gαq/11, and Gα12/13 activation.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 are supported by Videos 1-3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, which demonstrate the imaging capability of the platform. This extends the utility of EMTA beyond plate-based measurements to include spatial information.

result: EMTA shows significantly larger assay windows compared to BRET assays based on Gαβγ dissociation for six Gα subunits tested across eight receptors.
evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by direct side-by-side comparison data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5. The comparison with established methods (Galés et al., 2005, 2006; Olsen et al., 2020) demonstrates improved sensitivity of the EMTA platform.

result: The Gαs biosensor, based on dissociation from the plasma membrane, was validated using lithocholic acid stimulation of GPBA receptor and cholera toxin, showing concentration-dependent decreases in ebBRET that correlated with cAMP production and were selective (unaffected by UBO-QIC or PTX).
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2D. The validation includes agonist stimulation, direct G protein activation with CTX, correlation with downstream signaling (cAMP), and pharmacological selectivity testing, providing comprehensive validation of the Gs sensor.

result: The study profiled 100 therapeutically relevant human GPCRs across 15 signaling pathways (12 Gα subtypes and 3 βarrestin conditions), generating 1500 pathway-specific concentration-response curves.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 and C15 describe the scope of the profiling study, which is documented in Supplementary files 2-3 and Figure 3. The quantitative description (1500 curves from 100 receptors × 15 pathways) is mathematically consistent and supported by the comprehensive dataset presented.

result: Analysis of G protein family coupling revealed that 29% of receptors coupled to only one family, while 36%, 25%, and 10% coupled to 2, 3, or 4 families respectively. Gi/o showed the highest selectivity (27% exclusive coupling) compared to G12/13 (0%), Gq/11 (2.4%), and Gs (9.1%).
evaluation: Claims C45-C52 present quantitative analysis of the coupling data shown in Figure 4A-B. The percentages are internally consistent and sum appropriately. The finding that Gi/o shows highest selectivity while other families show more promiscuity is clearly supported by the data visualization.

result: Gi/o family members were most commonly activated (89% of receptors), while Gs (33%), G12/13 (49%), and Gq/11 excluding Gα15 (45%) showed lower activation frequencies. Gα15 was activated by 81% of receptors, consistent with its promiscuous coupling.
evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C. The high frequency of Gi/o activation and the promiscuity of Gα15 are consistent with known GPCR signaling biology and are clearly demonstrated in the dataset.

result: Intra-family coupling selectivity was observed, with 33% of Gi/o-coupled receptors activating only a subpopulation of the family. For Gq/11, only 44% activated all members, 45% activated only Gα15, and 11% engaged 2-3 members. Specific examples include 5-HT2B activating only GαoB and Gαz, and GPR65 selectively activating GαoB.
evaluation: Claims C58-C65 describe subtype selectivity within G protein families, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3. The specific examples (C62-C65) provide concrete illustrations of the selectivity patterns observed in the comprehensive dataset.

result: βarrestin recruitment analysis showed that 22% of receptors did not recruit βarrestin 1 or 2 even with GRK2 overexpression. Among receptors recruiting βarrestins, 92.3% recruited both isoforms in the presence of GRK2, while only 1.3% and 6.4% selectively recruited βarrestin1 or βarrestin2, respectively. GRK2 overexpression potentiated βarrestin2 recruitment for 68% of receptors.
evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D and Supplementary files 2-3. The data reveal limited isoform selectivity and the importance of GRK2 expression levels, providing insights into βarrestin recruitment patterns across the receptor panel.

result: Comparative analysis revealed 64% and 69% identity of couplings between EMTA and Inoue's or GtP datasets, respectively, with each dataset reporting unique couplings.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by comparative analysis presented in Supplementary file 4A-B. The moderate concordance (64-69%) is acknowledged along with differences, which are attributed to methodological variations. The authors provide appropriate context for interpreting these differences.

result: Newly identified G12/13 and G15 couplings were validated using orthogonal assays. FP and CysLT2 receptors activated G12/13 as confirmed by YM-254890-insensitive Rho and ezrin activation. EP2 and κOR receptors coupled to G15, and α2AAR and V2 receptors showed YM-254890-insensitive calcium responses upon Gα15 expression.
evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are supported by validation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B. The use of orthogonal assays (Rho/ezrin activation, calcium mobilization) and pharmacological tools (YM-254890 selectivity) provides strong validation of novel couplings identified by EMTA.

result: EMTA detected constitutive receptor activity and inverse agonism. Increasing A1 receptor expression led to receptor-dependent basal Gαi2 activation that was dose-dependently decreased by the inverse agonist DPCPX. Similarly, CB1 showed constitutive Gz activation that was completely blocked by rimonabant.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A. The receptor-dependent increase in basal activity and its reversal by inverse agonists demonstrate the platform's ability to detect constitutive activity. However, the authors acknowledge potential confounding from adenosine in culture medium for A1 (addressed in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

result: EMTA detected biased signaling of angiotensin receptor ligands. Angiotensin analogs (SII, saralasin, TRV027) showed biased signaling by promoting efficient βarrestin2 recruitment but marginal or no Gαq, Gαi2, or Gα13 activation compared to angiotensin II, which activated all pathways.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by data in Figure 5B with citations to prior work (Namkung et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2003). The platform successfully recapitulates known biased signaling profiles, validating its utility for detecting functional selectivity.

result: EMTA identified altered functional selectivity in naturally occurring GPR17 variants. The Asp128Asn variant showed WT-like Gαi2 activity but lost Gαq and βarrestin2 activation, while the Arg129His variant showed increased constitutive βarrestin2 recruitment and loss of Gαi2 and Gαq signaling.
evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C. The differential effects of variants at adjacent positions in the E/DRY motif demonstrate the platform's ability to detect subtle changes in functional selectivity resulting from single amino acid substitutions.

result: A combined Gz/G15 biosensor captured activation of 95% of receptors (73% activating Gαz, 81% activating Gα15) and successfully detected 24 GPCRs in a safety panel associated with adverse drug reactions.
evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citation to Bowes et al., 2012. The high coverage (95%) and successful application to a safety panel demonstrate the practical utility of this combined sensor for screening applications.

result: The Gz/G15 sensor detected ligand cross-reactivity: dopamine and serotonin activated α2AAR, noradrenaline and serotonin activated D2, and acetylcholine activated CB1/CB2. These were confirmed using selective antagonists (eticlopride for D2, WB4101 for α2AAR).
evaluation: Claims C91-C97 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6B-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The use of selective antagonists and comparison between endogenous and heterologous receptor expression provides strong evidence for direct cross-reactivity, consistent with prior reports (Roth et al., 2004; Sánchez-Soto et al., 2016).

result: CB1 activation by acetylcholine was indirect (trans-activation), involving secretion of an endogenous cannabinoid ligand following Gq/11 activation by endogenous muscarinic receptors. This was demonstrated by sensitivity to both CB inverse agonist AM-630 and cholinergic antagonist atropine, and by UBO-QIC blocking acetylcholine- but not WIN55,212-2-mediated activation.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101 are supported by pharmacological dissection experiments in Figure 6C. The differential effects of antagonists and the requirement for Gq/11 activity provide strong evidence for the proposed trans-activation mechanism, which has physiological precedent (Kim et al., 2002).

result: EMTA provides direct real-time measurement of proximal signaling events (Gα activation and βarrestin recruitment) with lower amplification than assays based on downstream effector enzymatic activity or artificial detection systems, reducing the risk of pathway cross-talk.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 describe conceptual advantages of the EMTA platform with support from citation to Mancini et al., 2015 regarding cross-talk issues. While these are logical inferences about the platform's design rather than direct experimental findings, they are well-reasoned and supported by the platform's architecture.

result: EMTA detected endogenous GPCR signaling in multiple cell types including HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, and HL-60 cells, demonstrating activation of endogenous Gi/o by FPR2 in HL-60 cells and PAR2 in HEK293 cells.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 7A-D. The ability to detect endogenous receptor and G protein activation in diverse cell types demonstrates the platform's versatility and applicability beyond heterologous expression systems.

result: EMTA was validated for detecting constitutive activity, inverse agonism, biased signaling, and polypharmacology.
evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are summary statements supported by the detailed experimental validations in C79-C101. Each capability is demonstrated with specific examples and appropriate controls, establishing EMTA as a comprehensive platform for studying diverse pharmacological phenomena.

result: The profiling revealed great diversity of coupling profiles ranging from exquisite selectivity to broad promiscuity.
evaluation: Claim C16 is a summary statement supported by the detailed quantitative analyses in C45-C65. The heatmap in Figure 3B and radial graphs in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 visually demonstrate this diversity across the 100 receptor panel.

result: The EMTA platform could be amenable for high-throughput screening of small molecules and biologics, allowing discovery of functionally selective molecules or GPCR deorphanization campaigns.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are speculative statements about future applications. While the platform's capabilities support these potential uses, no high-throughput screening or deorphanization data are presented. These represent reasonable extrapolations but are not experimentally demonstrated in the current work.

result: Background claims establishing the importance of GPCRs as drug targets, G protein classification, promiscuous coupling, ligand-directed selectivity, and the therapeutic potential of biased signaling.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are introductory statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Hauser et al., 2017; Namkung et al., 2018; Quoyer et al., 2013; Azzi et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2003; Galandrin et al., 2007; Kenakin, 2019). These provide necessary context for the study.
